rules.title: Massachusetts limit on upfront charges by lessors (application fee ban)
rules.requirement: Before a tenancy begins, a lessor may not require payment of anything except first month's rent, last month's rent, a security deposit, and a lock-change fee. Application, pet, cleaning, amenity and other charges are forbidden for landlords. Requiring an applicant to pay a third-party screening service is also risky. Licensed brokers may charge fees under separate broker rules.
rules.key_value: Only first, last, security deposit and locks may be charged before tenancy; application fees barred for lessors; treble damages and attorney's fees awarded in Perry v. Equity Residential (per the document)

coverage.summary: Applies to lessors (landlords) of rental housing in Massachusetts; licensed brokers are treated separately.

rules.exemptions: Licensed brokers may charge fees if they comply with 254 CMR 7 (written disclosure of fee amount, time and manner of payment, whether contingent on a lease, signed by applicant at first personal meeting). A landlord who is also a broker is uncertain; a separate bona fide brokerage operation was allowed in Samia v. McElaney (Housing Court, 1983, non-binding).
rules.effective_date_note: Source says the law has been in effect since the 1970s; no specific date stated.
rules.quoted_span: It states that prior to the beginning of a tenancy, no lessor may require payment for anything except first, last, security, and locks (MGL Ch 186 Section 15B).
rules.review_note: Secondary source (landlord association blog); statute section not quoted directly. Brokers' separate fee rules (254 CMR 7) are described as an exception, not a separate record.

result.doc_summary: A Massachusetts Landlords association article explaining that under G.L. c. 186, § 15B landlords may charge only first month, last month, security deposit and lock fees before a tenancy, so application and other fees are barred. Licensed brokers may charge fees under 254 CMR 7 with written disclosure. The article discusses risks of requiring tenants to pay third-party screening services, landlord-brokers, and the Perry v. Equity Residential, Woodruff v. Niles and Samia v. McElaney cases.
